name: Tomas Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run six hundred ewes on hill land, part of it ours and most of it common grazing, which is open hill shared with four other farms. In November the rams go in with the ewes, so I'm checking them every day, and the rest is moving sheep, mending walls and feeding hay to the older ewes on the low ground. My wife Marta is a teaching assistant at the village school, and she does lambing with me every spring on her holidays.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like gathering the hill with the dogs on a clear morning, when you can see three valleys and the sheep come down like water. What wears me out is the price of wool, which costs more to shear than it's worth, and the weather, which on the hill is always worse than the forecast.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use much technology up there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: More than you'd think. I've got a drone to find sheep in the gullies, and I use an AI assistant every day, for the lambing records, the grant forms and asking about worming plans. Some of the older men laugh at me, but it saves me hours of walking, and my knees are fifty-eight too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the next five years, one at a time. Here's the first. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool and every hill farmer should use it. I've shown a few of the younger lads at the mart how I use it for grant forms. I'd say it after chapel too, though the older ones there would shake their heads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't change the real problem. Lamb prices are poor, wool's worthless, and the grants we rely on keep changing. A better search engine makes the paperwork quicker, but it doesn't make a hill pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using it every day and push it a bit further, maybe using it to find buyers for lamb direct, in the first few months. I'd look into a few of those virtual fencing collars, the ones that steer sheep with a sound, if I could get a grant. Otherwise, I'd be careful, because there's barely three weeks of money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit restless. I like trying things, but the hill still doesn't pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said grants keep changing. What happens if one stops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half our income is the hill payment, for keeping the land in good order. If that stopped, I'd be selling ewes to pay the feed bill, and you don't get a hill flock back once it's gone. The sheep learn the hill from their mothers, it's called being hefted, and you can't buy that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the drone.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I bought it secondhand off a lad in town for four hundred. Last winter it found eleven ewes stuck in a snow drift behind the old sheepfold, and I'd never have seen them from the track. Marta calls it my flying dog.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a good tool and every hill farmer should use it. I've shown younger lads at the mart how I use it for grant forms, and I'd say so after chapel too.
S0.think: I really think it doesn't fix the real problem of poor lamb prices, worthless wool and changing grants. It makes paperwork quicker but doesn't make a hill pay.
S0.do: Keeps using AI daily and tries using it to find direct lamb buyers in the first few months. Looks into virtual fencing collars if a grant covers them, while staying careful with barely three weeks of money.
S0.feel: Fine but restless, liking new things while the hill still doesn't pay.
S0.quote: The sheep learn the hill from their mothers, it's called being hefted, and you can't buy that.
S0.fieldNote: He's an eager AI and drone user, unusual among the older hill farmers he mentions. The hill payment is half his income, and losing the hefted flock is his deepest fear. He mixes tradition and technology without seeing any conflict.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a pity it's slow, because hill farming needs help now, not in ten years. I'd say the young ones should learn the hill with the dogs first, and the gadgets after. That's how you get a proper shepherd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit frustrated, because I'm curious and I want to see what's coming. But fewer beginners is the real worry. There's only one young shepherd in our valley under thirty, and if he goes, the common grazing has nobody to look after it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep trying new tools, maybe the collars on a hundred ewes by spring if a grant came through. I'd take on a young lad from the village as a sort of apprentice, a couple of days a week, to learn the dogs and the drone together. I'd ask the chapel and the young farmers' club to help find him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Impatient for myself, worried for the valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who is the one young shepherd under thirty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rhys, he's twenty-six, works for the farm across the beck. He's good with a dog but he talks about leaving for a job in the quarry, because it pays better. If he goes, I'm the youngest one on that hill at fifty-eight, and that's not a good sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd teach an apprentice the dogs and the drone together. Why both?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the drone finds them, but the dog brings them home. A drone can't push four hundred ewes down a hillside. You need both, and a young one who only learns one will be half a shepherd.

S1.say: I'd say it's a pity it's slow, because hill farming needs help now. The young should learn the hill with dogs first and gadgets after.
S1.think: I'm privately frustrated it's slow, because I'm curious. The real worry is fewer beginners, with only one shepherd under thirty in the valley.
S1.do: Puts virtual fencing collars on a hundred ewes by spring if a grant comes through. Takes on a young village lad as an apprentice two days a week to learn dogs and drone together, finding him through chapel and the young farmers' club.
S1.feel: Impatient for himself and worried for the valley.
S1.quote: Because the drone finds them, but the dog brings them home.
S1.fieldNote: He wants young people trained in both dogs and drones, which captures how he blends old and new. His concern is that the valley is running out of young shepherds like Rhys. His traditional values show through chapel and community.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say office people will have to adapt like farmers always have, and quickly. I'd tell them to come up the hill and see what real work is, half joking. And I'd say the politicians shouting won't help, people need to get stuck in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't touch my sheep, but it could touch the grants. If the government offices are run by AI assistants, the forms might get faster, or they might get harder, I honestly don't know. And Marta says the school office has already had cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get better at using the assistants myself, maybe every grant form and every mart booking, so I'm ready if the government side changes. I'd help a few of the older farmers with theirs, because they won't touch it. And I'd keep the apprentice going if I could afford it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but ready. I'd rather know the tool than be scared of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd help the older farmers with their forms. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Gwilym on the next farm, he's seventy-four and still on the hill every day. He does his forms with a pen and a magnifying glass. If they go online-only with AI, he'll be lost, and I'd sit at his kitchen table and do them with him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you charge him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Charge Gwilym? He pulled my tractor out of a ditch in the snow when I was twenty. You don't charge neighbours, you just do it, and one day he'll do something for me.

S2.say: I'd say office people will have to adapt quickly, like farmers always have, and I'd half-jokingly invite them up the hill. Shouting politicians won't help; people need to get stuck in.
S2.think: I really think it doesn't touch my sheep but could change the grants, and I don't know whether AI-run offices would make forms faster or harder. Marta's school office has already had cuts.
S2.do: Uses AI assistants for every grant form and mart booking so he's ready if government offices change. Helps older farmers like Gwilym with their forms for free and keeps the apprentice if he can afford it.
S2.feel: Uneasy but ready, preferring to know the tool than fear it.
S2.quote: Charge Gwilym? He pulled my tractor out of a ditch in the snow when I was twenty.
S2.fieldNote: He sees himself as the bridge between new tools and old neighbours like Gwilym. He's honest that he doesn't know whether AI-run offices would help or hurt the grants. His traditional values show as neighbourliness, not politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains should go to people who work and build things, not just the ones with shares. I'd say help people get back to work with training, not handouts. And I'd say the countryside should get its share, because we keep the land in order for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried about the house prices most. Rich people will want holiday homes in the valley, and the young ones like Rhys will never afford to stay. And if the government's in crisis, the hill payments might get cut while they argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the assistant to look at selling lamb direct to the new people moving in, maybe as boxes, in the first six months. I'd talk to the chapel and the village about putting some houses aside for local young families. And I'd keep the apprentice on, even if it meant selling a few more lambs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the valley emptying out. The sheep are fine, the people are the worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling lamb to the new people moving in, the same ones pricing out Rhys. Does that sit right with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not entirely, no. But if they're coming anyway, I'd rather they ate our lamb than something from the other side of the world. I'd use the money to keep the apprentice, so at least one young one stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the hill if the payments got cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have to cut the flock, maybe by a third, and the hill would start going to bracken and scrub. Once that happens, it takes years to bring back. People think a hill looks after itself, but it doesn't, it's been looked after for a thousand years.

S3.say: I'd say the gains should go to people who work and build things, through training, not handouts. The countryside deserves its share because we keep the land in order for everyone.
S3.think: I'm privately most worried about holiday homes pricing out young people like Rhys. A government in crisis might also cut the hill payments while it argues.
S3.do: Uses AI to sell lamb boxes direct to newcomers within six months. Works with chapel and village to set aside homes for local young families and keeps the apprentice even if it means selling more lambs.
S3.feel: Anxious about the valley emptying of people, though the sheep would be fine.
S3.quote: People think a hill looks after itself, but it doesn't, it's been looked after for a thousand years.
S3.fieldNote: He admitted that selling lamb to the people pricing out young locals doesn't sit right, but he'd use the money to keep an apprentice. His fear is the valley emptying and the hill going to bracken. Holiday homes and cut payments are his twin threats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on the hill could be a help, if they're used to keep families farming, not to replace them. I'd say I'd try one before I'd judge it. And I'd say we need apprenticeships so the young ones learn to run the robots and the dogs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm curious and scared in equal measure. A robot that could gather the hill or help with lambing would save my knees, and I'd want one. But if the big lowland farms run robot sheep flocks, our lamb price drops, and the hill's not worth farming at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get a robot or a robot dog on a trial or a grant, maybe in the second year, once there was one that could handle steep ground. I'd go straight to the young farmers' club and the college to push for courses on running them. And I'd keep the dogs, whatever happens, because I don't trust a machine in the fog on the tops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and worried at once, and more worried for the young ones than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your apprentice if robots came onto the hill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn the robots, but don't let go of the dogs. I'll fly a drone over the hill gladly. But if no young one ever learns to gather with a dog, the hill forgets us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a robot on a grant. With three weeks of savings, what if it went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd sell it and go back to the dogs, and I'd have lost a year. I'm not going to borrow for it, mind, Marta would have my hide. A grant or nothing.

S4.say: I'd say hill robots could help if they keep families farming instead of replacing them, and I'd try one before judging. We need apprenticeships so the young learn both robots and dogs.
S4.think: I'm privately curious and scared in equal measure, and I'd want a robot to save my knees. But lowland robot flocks would cut lamb prices until the hill isn't worth farming.
S4.do: Tries to get a robot or robot dog through a trial or grant in year two, once one can handle steep ground, refusing to borrow. Pushes the young farmers' club and college for courses on running robots and keeps his dogs.
S4.feel: Excited and worried at once, more for young people than for himself.
S4.quote: I'll fly a drone over the hill gladly. But if no young one ever learns to gather with a dog, the hill forgets us.
S4.fieldNote: He's eager to try robots but won't borrow, and he'd keep the dogs for fog on the tops. His deepest fear is losing the living knowledge of the hill. Even here, his thoughts went first to the young.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, because if lowland robot flocks make lamb cheap enough, nobody will pay to keep the hill farmed. What would help is a hill payment that's steady and pays for looking after the land, and apprenticeships that teach both dogs and machines. And grants for trying new tools, because we can't borrow at our age.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the sheepdog trials. We have one every August, and it's the best day of the year in the valley. If that goes, it's not just a hobby, it's how we pass the skills on.

headlineQuote: I'll fly a drone over the hill gladly. But if no young one ever learns to gather with a dog, the hill forgets us.
portrait: Tomas is 58 and runs six hundred ewes on hill land and common grazing, using a secondhand drone and an AI assistant every day while still gathering with his dogs. He's traditional, rooted in chapel, neighbours and the old ways of the hill, but he's the one who teaches the younger lads to use the new tools. His worries move from grants and paperwork to holiday homes pricing out young shepherds like Rhys. In the robot picture he'd happily try a robot on a grant, but fears cheap lowland lamb and a hill nobody knows how to gather.
biggestWorry: The robot picture, because cheap lowland robot flocks could make the hill not worth farming at all.
whatWouldHelp: A steady hill payment for looking after the land, apprenticeships teaching both dogs and machines, and grants rather than loans for new tools.
